explain.title: Scalars
explain.body: A scalar is that physical quantity which can be described completely by its magnitude only. Magnitude includes a number and an appropriate unit. Distance, length, time, speed, energy and temperature are examples of scalars. Scalar quantities can be added up like numbers.

explain.title: Vectors
explain.body: A vector is that physical quantity which needs magnitude as well as direction to describe it completely. Displacement, velocity, acceleration, weight and force are examples of vectors. Their directions must be considered when vectors are added.

explain.title: Drawing a vector
explain.body: A vector is drawn as a straight line with an arrowhead at one end. The length represents magnitude according to a suitable scale, while the arrow indicates direction. To specify direction, use reference axes and measure the angle from the appropriate axis.

explain.title: Adding vectors graphically

Measuring an angle from the wrong reference direction.

writtenQuestions.text: Describe different types of motion. Also give examples.
modelAnswer: There are three general types of motion: translatory, rotatory and vibratory.
If every particle of a body moves uniformly in the same direction, it is called translatory motion; the motion of a train or a car is an example.
Translatory motion can be linear, random or circular: a freely falling body is linear, a bee moving along an irregular path is random, and a Ferris wheel is circular.
If each point of a body moves around a fixed point (axis), the motion is called rotatory motion; an electric fan or a top is an example.
When a body repeats its to and fro motion about a fixed position, the motion is called vibratory motion; a swing is an example.

explain.title: Speed
explain.body: We are often interested to know how fast a body is moving. For this purpose, we have to find the distance covered in unit time which is known as speed. If a body covers a distance S in time t, its speed v will be written as: Speed = Distance/Time  v = S/t or S = vt. The speed is a scalar quantity.

explain.title: Average and instantaneous speed
explain.body: The speed of a vehicle that is shown by its speedometer at any instant is called instantaneous speed. Practically we make use of the average speed. It is defined as: Average speed = (Total distance covered)/(Total time taken) or v_av = S/t

explain.title: Velocity
explain.body: The net displacement of a body in unit time is called velocity. Average velocity = Displacement/Time or vector v_av = vector d/t. Velocity is a vector quantity. The direction of velocity vector v is the same as that of displacement vector d.

explain.title: Uniform and non-uniform velocity
explain.body: The velocity is said to be uniform if the speed and direction of a moving body does not change. If the speed or direction or both of them change, it is known as variable velocity or non-uniform velocity.

explain.title: What acceleration means

explain.title: Positive and negative acceleration

explain.title: Average acceleration

explain.title: Uniform and non-uniform acceleration
explain.body: If time rate of change of velocity is constant, the acceleration is said to be uniform. If anyone of the magnitude or direction or both of them changes it is called variable or non-uniform acceleration.

v_f = v_i + at.
S = v_i t + 1/2 at².
Height above ground = 45 + 1 = 46 m.
Answer: (30 m s⁻¹, 46 m).

explain.title: The equations of motion
explain.body: Your textbook gives these three equations: v_f = v_i + at; S = v_i t + 1/2 at²; 2aS = v_f² − v_i². Choose the equation that contains the quantities you know and the one you need to find.

explain.title: Assumptions
explain.body: Your textbook states: “Motion is always considered along a straight line”; “Only the magnitudes of vector quantities are used”; and “Acceleration is assumed to be uniform.” Make sure the situation fits these assumptions when using the equations.

explain.title: Direction and signs
explain.body: Your textbook states: “The direction of initial velocity is taken as positive. Other quantities which are in the direction of initial velocity are taken as positive. The quantities in the direction opposite to the initial velocity are taken as negative.” For a dropped object, choose a consistent direction for the calculation and give gravity the matching sign.

explain.title: Motion upward
explain.body: For a ball thrown upward, take upward as positive. Gravity then has a negative sign. At the highest point, the ball's velocity is zero for an instant, but its acceleration is still due to gravity.

mistakes: Using a positive sign for gravity when it acts opposite to the chosen positive direction.
Forgetting that a dropped object starts with v_i = 0.
Setting acceleration to zero at the highest point instead of setting the instantaneous velocity to zero.
Mixing units or leaving units out of the final answers.
Using an equation without showing substitution and working.

writtenQuestions.text: How equations of motion can be applied to the bodies moving under the action of gravity?
modelAnswer: Since freely falling bodies move vertically downwards in a straight line with uniform acceleration g, the three equations of motion can be applied.
Replace acceleration a by gravitational acceleration g in the equations of motion:
v_f = v_i + gt
S = v_i t + ½gt²
2gS = v_f² − v_i²
Take g positive downward; quantities opposite to the acceleration are negative.
For a body released from a height, vᵢ = 0.
For a body thrown vertically upward, g is negative and v_f = 0 at the highest point.

rubric.how: Take g positive downward and opposite-direction quantities as negative.

For an object thrown upward, use g = −10 m s⁻² and v_f = 0 at the highest point.

From first equation of motion, v_f = vᵢ + gt
Now from the third equation of motion, 2gS = v_f² − vᵢ²

explain.title: Gravitational acceleration
explain.body: Your textbook defines it this way: “When a body is falling freely under the action of gravity of the Earth, the acceleration acting on it is the gravitational acceleration and is denoted by g.” It also states: “The direction of gravitational acceleration is always downwards. Its value is 9.8 m s⁻², but for convenience we shall use the value of g as 10 m s⁻².”

explain.title: Equations for freely falling bodies
explain.body: The three equations of motion are used with a replaced by g: v_f = v_i + gt; S = v_i t + ½gt²; 2gS = v_f² − v_i². Choose the equation that includes the unknown you need.

explain.title: Choose signs carefully
explain.body: Use g as positive when downward is positive. Quantities in the opposite direction are negative. If a body is released from a height, vᵢ = 0. If it is thrown vertically upward, g is negative and the final velocity at the highest point is zero.

explain.title: Objects fall with the same acceleration
explain.body: Your textbook states: “Acceleration of free fall g is 10 m s⁻² for all objects.” The section also notes that light and heavier objects fall side by side through a vacuum.

mistakes: Using g = +10 m s⁻² for a body thrown upward; in that case use g = −10 m s⁻².
Forgetting that a body released from rest has vᵢ = 0.
Using a non-zero final velocity at the highest point; there v_f = 0.
Giving a velocity without a unit or using the wrong unit; velocity is measured in m s⁻¹ and acceleration in m s⁻².
Forgetting that the stated height for an upward-thrown object may be the rise above its starting point, not its height above the ground.

explain.title: Scalars and vectors
explain.body: A scalar has magnitude only. A vector has both magnitude and direction. Distance and speed are scalars; displacement, velocity and acceleration are vectors.

explain.title: Distance and displacement
explain.body: Distance is the total path travelled. Displacement is the change in position in a specified direction. Displacement magnitude cannot be greater than distance.

explain.title: Speed, velocity and acceleration
explain.body: Speed is distance per unit time. Velocity is displacement per unit time. Acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time.

explain.title: Motion graphs
explain.body: The gradient of a distance–time graph gives speed; the gradient of a displacement–time graph gives velocity. The gradient of a speed–time graph gives acceleration, and its area gives distance.

explain.title: Equations of motion
explain.body: For constant acceleration, use v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², or v² = u² + 2as. For motion under gravity, use g as the acceleration and keep the chosen direction and signs consistent.

mistakes: Treating distance and displacement as identical even when direction changes.
Calling velocity uniform just because speed is constant; direction must also stay constant.
Reading the gradient of a speed–time graph as distance; distance is the area under that graph.
Forgetting to convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ before using SI units in an equation.
Using the wrong sign for gravity or braking acceleration.
Leaving units out of a numerical answer or omitting the direction when it matters.

notes.title: Scalars, vectors and their representation
notes.answer: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction.
notes.explanation: Scalars are fully described by magnitude only. Vectors need both magnitude and direction. A vector can be shown by a straight line with an arrow: its length shows magnitude according to a scale, and the arrow shows direction.
notes.simple: A scalar tells you how much. A vector tells you how much and which way.
examples: 5 kg of mass is a scalar: the magnitude and unit describe it completely.
A velocity of 25 m s⁻¹ towards north is a vector: it has magnitude and direction.
steps: Identify whether the quantity needs direction as well as magnitude.
For a scalar, give its magnitude and unit.
For a vector, give its magnitude, unit and direction.
To draw a vector, choose a scale and draw a line with an arrow in the required direction.
notes.checkQuestion: What two things are needed to describe a vector completely?
notes.checkAnswer: A vector has magnitude and direction.

notes.title: Rest and motion depend on the observer
notes.answer: Rest or motion is decided by comparing an object's position with its surroundings.
notes.explanation: Rest and motion describe whether an object's position changes compared with its surroundings. The same object can be at rest compared with one observer and in motion compared with another.
notes.simple: Ask: “Is the object's position changing compared with this observer and these surroundings?” The answer may change when the observer changes.
examples: A parked motorcycle is at rest compared with a nearby tree.
A passenger sitting in a moving train is at rest compared with other passengers, but in motion compared with someone standing on the platform.
steps: Choose the object and the observer.
Compare the object's position with its surroundings.
If its position does not change, it is at rest with respect to those surroundings.
If its position continuously changes, it is in motion with respect to those surroundings.
notes.checkQuestion: A passenger is sitting in a moving train. Is the passenger at rest or in motion compared with someone standing on the platform?
notes.checkAnswer: The passenger is at rest with respect to the other passengers, but in motion with respect to the observer on the platform.

notes.title: Recognising types of motion
notes.answer: The three general types are translatory, rotatory, and vibratory motion.
notes.explanation: Motion is classified by how a body moves: it may move as a whole, turn around an axis, or move to and fro around a fixed position.
notes.simple: Look at the path or movement: straight, irregular, circular, turning around an axis, or to and fro.
steps: Notice how the body moves.
If every particle moves in the same direction, identify translatory motion and then check whether its path is straight, irregular, or circular.
If points of the body move around a fixed axis, identify rotatory motion.
If the body repeats a to-and-fro movement about a fixed position, identify vibratory motion.
notes.checkQuestion: What type of motion does an electric fan show?

notes.title: Distance and Displacement
notes.answer: Distance is the length of actual path of the motion. Displacement is the shortest distance from the initial to the final position, with direction from the initial position to the final position.
notes.explanation: Distance tells how much actual path an object travels. Displacement tells how far and in what direction it is from its starting position to its final position.
notes.simple: Distance is the route taken. Displacement is the straight way from where you started to where you ended, including its direction.
examples: A car may travel 320 km along roads from Lahore to Multan; that is its distance travelled.
If the car’s starting and ending points are A and B, the straight, directed line from A to B represents its displacement.
steps: Identify the actual path travelled: its length is the distance.
Identify the initial and final positions.
Join these positions with a straight line and show its direction from initial to final: this is the displacement.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the difference between distance and displacement?
notes.checkAnswer: Distance is the length of the actual path; displacement is the shortest directed distance from the initial position to the final position.

notes.title: Speed and Velocity
notes.answer: Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Average velocity is displacement divided by time and has a direction.
notes.explanation: Speed tells how much distance is covered per unit time. Velocity also tells the direction of motion, so it depends on displacement rather than distance. For example, a car moving north at 70 km h⁻¹ has speed 70 km h⁻¹ and velocity 70 km h⁻¹ north.
notes.simple: Speed tells how fast something moves. Velocity tells how fast it moves and in which direction.
steps: For average speed, divide total distance by total time.
For average velocity, divide displacement by time.
Give the direction when stating velocity.
notes.checkQuestion: What extra information does velocity give that speed does not?

notes.title: Acceleration
notes.explanation: Acceleration tells us how quickly velocity changes. A change in velocity may be a change in speed, direction, or both.
notes.simple: Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes. If velocity gets smaller, acceleration is negative.
examples: A car speeds up from rest: its velocity increases, so it has positive acceleration.
A moving car brakes and slows down: its velocity decreases, so it has negative acceleration.
steps: Find the change in velocity: v_f − v_i.
Divide the change in velocity by the time taken: a_av = (v_f − v_i)/t.
Write the answer in m s⁻².
notes.checkQuestion: A body changes velocity from 4 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ in 3 s. What is its average acceleration?
notes.checkAnswer: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken: a_av = (v_f − v_i)/t.

notes.title: Reading distance-time graphs
notes.answer: A distance-time graph shows the relation between distance S and time t taken by a moving body.
notes.explanation: A distance-time graph shows how distance changes with time. Its slope tells us the speed: a straight rising line means uniform speed, a curved line can show changing speed, and a horizontal line means the body is at rest.
notes.simple: Look at how the graph changes as you move to the right. If distance rises evenly, speed is uniform. If distance does not change, the body is not moving.
examples: If a car travels 1.2 km each minute, its distance-time graph is a straight rising line.
If distance stays at 1.2 km as time passes, the graph is horizontal and the car is at rest.
steps: Put time t on the x-axis and distance S on the y-axis.
Choose a suitable scale for each axis.
Plot each time-distance pair.
Join the plotted points and interpret the graph shape.
notes.checkQuestion: What does a horizontal distance-time graph show?

notes.title: Gradient of a Distance-Time Graph
notes.answer: The gradient of a distance-time graph is equal to the average speed of the body.
notes.explanation: The gradient of a distance-time graph tells you the average speed during a time interval. Find it by dividing the change in distance by the change in time.
notes.simple: Gradient tells you how much distance changes for each unit of time.
examples: If distance changes by 12 m in 3 s, gradient = 12/3 = 4 m s⁻¹.
A horizontal distance-time line has gradient 0, so the body is at rest.
steps: Find the change in distance: S₂ − S₁.
Find the change in time: t₂ − t₁.
Divide the change in distance by the change in time.
Write the result with suitable units.
notes.checkQuestion: A body covers 15 m in 3 s. What is the gradient of its distance-time graph?

notes.title: Reading a speed-time graph
notes.answer: A speed-time graph is a graph between speed v and time t. A straight line rising upward shows uniform acceleration; a horizontal line shows constant speed.
notes.explanation: A speed-time graph shows how an object's speed changes with time. The shape of the line helps us describe the motion.
notes.simple: Look at the line: rising means speed is increasing; horizontal means speed is unchanged.
examples: A straight line rising from the origin shows speed increasing by the same amount in equal time intervals.
A horizontal line shows that speed stays the same as time passes.
steps: Put time t on the x-axis and speed v on the y-axis.
Mark the speed at each time.
Join the points and observe the shape of the line.
notes.checkQuestion: What kind of motion is shown by a straight line rising upward on a speed-time graph when speed increases equally every second?
notes.checkAnswer: A horizontal line parallel to the time axis represents constant speed.

notes.title: Gradient of a Speed-Time Graph
notes.explanation: The gradient of a speed-time graph tells us the average acceleration. Find it by dividing the change in speed by the time taken.
notes.simple: A steeper speed-time graph means speed is changing more quickly. A flat graph means speed is not changing.
examples: If speed changes from 4 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ in 3 s, the gradient is (10 − 4)/3 = 2 m s⁻².
If speed stays constant, the speed-time graph is horizontal and its gradient is zero.
steps: Find the change in speed: 18 − 6 = 12 m s⁻¹.
Divide the change in speed by the time: 12/4 = 3 m s⁻².
State the gradient as 3 m s⁻².
notes.checkQuestion: A body's speed changes from 6 m s⁻¹ to 18 m s⁻¹ in 4 s. What is the gradient?
notes.checkAnswer: The average acceleration is 2 m s⁻².

notes.title: Finding Distance from a Speed-Time Graph
notes.answer: The area under a speed-time graph up to the time axis is numerically equal to the distance covered by the object.
notes.explanation: A speed-time graph shows how an object's speed changes with time. The area between the graph and the time axis gives the distance covered. For constant speed, this area is a rectangle; for speed increasing uniformly from zero, it is a triangle.
notes.simple: Think of the area under a speed-time graph as the distance travelled. Find the area of the shape below the graph and above the time axis.
examples: At a constant speed of 5 m/s for 4 s, the distance is the rectangular area: 5 × 4 = 20 m.
If speed increases uniformly from 0 to 6 m/s in 3 s, the distance is the triangular area: 1/2 × 6 × 3 = 9 m.
steps: Identify the shape under the speed-time graph.
Find its area using the correct formula.
The area is numerically equal to the distance covered.
notes.checkQuestion: An object moves at a constant speed of 4 m/s for 3 s. What distance does it cover?

notes.title: Solving problems for motion under gravity
notes.answer: Use the equations of motion with acceleration due to gravity and a consistent choice of signs.
notes.explanation: For motion under gravity, use the equations of motion with acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻², as used for the answers in your textbook. Choose positive and negative directions consistently, then substitute the known quantities.
notes.simple: Gravity changes an object's velocity as it falls or rises. Use the motion equations and give quantities the correct signs.
steps: Write down the known quantities and the quantity to find.
Choose a positive direction and assign signs to the other quantities.
Select the equation containing the known quantities and the unknown.
Substitute the values, calculate, and write the answer with its unit.
notes.checkQuestion: A stone is dropped from rest and falls for 3 s. Take g = 10 m s⁻². What is its final velocity?
notes.checkAnswer: t = 3 s; v_f = 30 m s⁻¹ downward.

notes.title: Using equations for free fall
notes.answer: For a freely falling object released from rest, vᵢ = 0 and g = +10 m s⁻² when downward is positive.
notes.explanation: For free fall, use the equations of motion with acceleration replaced by g. Take g = 10 m s⁻² downward as positive. If an object is thrown upward, take g = −10 m s⁻².
notes.simple: A freely falling object speeds up because Earth’s gravity pulls it downward. Use g = 10 m s⁻², and choose signs to match the direction of motion.
examples: A body dropped from rest for 3 s falls 45 m: S = 0 × 3 + ½ × 10 × 3² = 45 m.
An arrow thrown upward at 30 m s⁻¹ takes 3 s to reach its highest point: 0 = 30 − 10t, so t = 3 s.
steps: Write down the known values, including the direction of motion.
Use vᵢ = 0 if the object is released from rest.
Take g as positive downward; for an object thrown upward, take g as negative.
Choose the equation of motion that contains the unknown you need.
Substitute the values and give the answer with its unit.
notes.checkQuestion: A stone is dropped from rest. What is its initial velocity, and which way is g positive?
notes.checkAnswer: For a body dropped from rest, vᵢ = 0 and g = 10 m s⁻² downward.

notes.title: Describing motion
notes.answer: Kinematics describes motion using distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration.
notes.explanation: Kinematics describes motion and how position, speed, velocity and acceleration change with time. Graphs and equations of motion help us describe and calculate these changes.
notes.simple: Kinematics is the study of motion. It tells us how far and in which direction something moves, how fast it moves, and how its motion changes.
examples: A car travelling at constant speed in a straight line has constant velocity.
A ball thrown vertically upward has zero velocity for an instant at its highest point, but its acceleration is still downward.
steps: Choose a positive direction and keep it consistent.
Use distance for the total path covered and displacement for the change in position.
Use speed or velocity to describe how quickly position changes.
Use acceleration to describe how quickly velocity changes.
For calculations, choose an equation of motion that includes the known quantities and the quantity required.
notes.checkQuestion: What does the gradient of a speed–time graph represent?
notes.checkAnswer: Speed is the gradient of a distance–time graph; acceleration is the gradient of a speed–time graph.

quiz.stem: Which quantity is a scalar?
rationales: Mass is a scalar because it is described by magnitude only.
Displacement is a vector because it has magnitude and direction.
Force is a vector because it has magnitude and direction.
Velocity is a vector because it has magnitude and direction.

quiz.stem: Which quantity can be completely described by magnitude only?
rationales: Temperature is a scalar and does not need a direction.
Weight is a vector because it is a force with a direction.
Acceleration is a vector because its direction is needed.
Velocity is a vector because its direction is needed.

quiz.stem: What information is needed to describe a vector completely?
rationales: Magnitude only is enough for a scalar, not a vector.
Direction alone does not tell how large the vector is.
A vector needs both magnitude and direction.
A number without a unit does not fully specify a physical quantity.

quiz.stem: In a graphical representation of a vector, what represents its magnitude?
rationales: The line length represents magnitude according to the chosen scale.
The arrowhead indicates the vector's direction.
The origin is a reference point and does not show magnitude.
An angle can specify direction but does not by itself represent magnitude.

quiz.stem: Which drawing is used to represent a vector graphically?
options: A straight line without an arrow
